source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE
finding: Benchmark of 324 Codeforces problems, each with a subtly wrong submission. The model must write code that prints an input where the wrong code differs from the right code. Best reasoning agents refute under 9% of wrong submissions.
numbers: 324 problems by 304 programmers, 34 topics. o3-mini (high) with code execution: under 9% success, while its Codeforces Elo implies it solves about 48% of the same problems from scratch (DeepSeek-R1 about 44%).
quote: can create counterexamples for only < 9% of incorrect solutions
limits: Competitive-programming domain with an exact oracle (run both programs). Dynamic benchmark, numbers shift as it updates.
agent_relevance: Finding the one discriminating input is much harder than solving the problem. Do not assume S7 test search is easy for the model; give it a runnable oracle.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE
finding: Giving the model the correct solution does not close the gap. An agent with up to 10 code runs gained little except DeepSeek-R1. Execution feedback removed malformed tests (R1 and V3 went from 45 and 36 invalid outputs to 0) but not wrong reasoning.
numbers: Table 1 cells run from about 0.9% to 9.3% across 5 models and 4 setups (zero-shot, few-shot, with correct solution, ReAct agent).
limits: The PDF table text was garbled, so only abstract and prose numbers are recorded as reliable.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback fixes format errors, not the harder step of reasoning about where a rule breaks.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE
finding: Explicitly prompting a randomised search (write an input generator and a brute-force solver, compare outputs) helped chat models a little and hurt reasoning models. With the correct solution as oracle the search reached up to 15.1%.
numbers: RandSearch: V3 4.0, Flash-Thinking 3.7, R1 4.0, o3-mini(high) 8.3. RandSearch Oracle: V3 15.1, Flash 7.7, R1 9.9. On average 35% of RandSearch runs ended in a wrong counterexample; of these 86% came from wrong brute-force code and 14% from invalid test format.
limits: The model-written brute-force reference is itself the weak link.
agent_relevance: A model-written reference is unreliable. For S7 use the competing candidate programs as the oracle, not a third model-written one.

source: Sinha, Goel, Kumaraguru, Geiping, Bethge, Prabhu (2025) Can Language Models Falsify? REFUTE
finding: Different strategies solve different cases, and success is not predictable from difficulty or author skill.
numbers: o3-mini RandSearch refuted 6% distinct submissions that prompting and agent modes missed (3% new when the correct solution was supplied). Success on submissions that passed all initial tests: 4% +/- 1%.
limits: Small absolute numbers.
agent_relevance: Mixing test-finding strategies adds coverage; one method is not enough.

source: Yang, Kuang, Xia, Zhao (2025) TestCase-Eval
finding: 500 Codeforces problems and 100,000 human solutions, 19 LLMs. Task 2 (Fault Exposure) asks for one test that breaks a given wrong program. Best model Qwen3-32B reaches 43.8%; human experts 93.3%.
numbers: Fault exposure: Qwen3-32B 43.8, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 41.6, Qwen3-8B 41.3, GPT-4.1 36.5, GPT-4.1-mini 33.6, GPT-4o 31.7. Humans 93.3. GPT-4.1 by failure type: wrong answer 42.0, runtime error 35.4, time limit 20.9, memory limit 25.1.
limits: Single-shot generation of one test per wrong program.
agent_relevance: A gap of about 50 points to humans. Reasoning models do better at targeting a specific wrong program.

source: Yang, Kuang, Xia, Zhao (2025) TestCase-Eval
finding: Chain-of-thought beat direct output for test generation. Reasoning models beat general models on both tasks. Python solutions were easier to break than C++ or Java. Many draws raise coverage a lot.
numbers: Fault coverage: Qwen3-32B 50.8 cov@1 and 95.7 cov@20, versus GPT-4.1 45.3 cov@1 and 80.0 cov@20.
limits: CoT vs direct effect size is only in a figure, not read.
agent_relevance: Think before proposing the test, and draw many cheap candidate tests then run them.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath: Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (ICML 2025)
finding: University-level benchmark of 1,216 statements where the key step is a counterexample. Math-tuned open models judge truth poorly and rarely give a valid example; reasoning models do far better.
numbers: 1,216 statement-rationale pairs, 4 fields. Judgement F1: most open models near 30; Qwen2.5-Math-72B 41.8; GPT-4o 59.0; o1-preview 60.1; Qwen-max 58.9; Claude 3.7 Sonnet 64.8; Gemini 2.5 Pro 77.0; DeepSeek-R1 80.7.
limits: Rationale quality judged by GPT-4o (about 93.5% agreement with humans). Commercial-row model names read from a garbled table; R1 = 80.7 is confirmed in the text.
agent_relevance: Counterexample reasoning is a separate skill that drill-style math training does not give.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath: Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (ICML 2025)
finding: Saying 'false' is not the same as giving a valid counterexample. Strict and loose rationale scores are far below judgement scores.
numbers: Strict / loose (%): DeepSeek-R1 54.2 / 65.3; Gemini 2.5 Pro 65.1 / 75.7; Claude 3.7 45.0 / 52.5; o1-preview 39.8 / 40.9; GPT-4o 19.7 / 21.3; Qwen2.5-Math-72B 38.9 / 41.6; MetaMath 7B 0.4 / 0.7. Example-giving rate: R1 86.8, GPT-4o 44.7, MetaMath 26.5, rho-math 18.3.
limits: LLM-judged.
agent_relevance: Require the witness, not only the verdict; a verdict with no checkable example is weak evidence.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMath: Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (ICML 2025)
finding: Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct on 1,025 filtered counterexample samples gave small gains on its own benchmark and gains elsewhere.
numbers: Own benchmark: F1 about 39.4 to 41.1 and examples 79.0 to 79.4 (some metrics slightly worse). Out of distribution: AIME 2024 20.0 to 30.0, MATH 80.5 to 87.9 (row labels assumed: base 7B vs SFT 7B).
limits: Training result with partly garbled table; one run.
agent_relevance: Suggests counterexample practice transfers, but our agent does not train.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs play Wason's hidden-rule game (propose a triple, get yes/no, then guess the rule, up to 45 turns). They often propose tests that fit their own guess. Success runs from 6% to 78%, and more disconfirming tests go with more success.
numbers: Success 6% to 78% over 11 models. Non-thinking vs thinking baselines: Qwen3-8B 6% vs 21%; Qwen3-14B 23% vs about 34-36%; Qwen3-32B 33% vs 41%; LLaMA-3.3-70B 21%. I:C (incompatible to compatible test ratio) correlates positively with success.
limits: Synthetic rule sets from LLM-generated rules plus human-derived rules; integer triples in [-99,100]. Thinking mode lifts success without a consistent rise in I:C, so the gain is not only from falsifying.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of the human 2-4-6 finding. The agent needs a forced step that tests what would break its guess.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Counterexample prompting (Think-in-Opposites, TiO) lifts rule discovery from 42% to 56% on average. Gains are large for thinking models and small for non-thinking models. A second prompt (Dual-Goal) helped thinking models but hurt non-thinking ones.
numbers: Paired permutation tests (50,000). Thinking: TiO success +0.123, I:C +0.168 (p<2e-5); Dual-Goal +0.148. Non-thinking: TiO +0.063 (p=0.0033), I:C +0.020 (n.s.); Dual-Goal -0.060 (p=0.0065). Qwen3-32B thinking 41% to 61%; Qwen3-8B 21% to 36%; LLaMA-3.3-70B 21% to 38%.
limits: Prompt effect depends on model type. Blicket task: effect on non-thinking models substantially smaller.
agent_relevance: Add the falsification instruction at S7, expect more help for reasoning-mode models, and test per model.

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Fine-tuning on TiO-induced behaviour made falsifying tests the default and carried over to a new task (Blicket detector), though less than prompting inside the new task.
numbers: Same-scale distillation: Qwen3-8B 21% to 35%, Qwen3-32B 41% to 64%. Cross-scale (32B teacher to 8B) 44%, about tripling the base 8B's success and more than doubling I:C.
limits: Training result. Blicket hypotheses have no clean opposite, so TiO fits less well there.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect is not one-task; supports a reusable S7 step.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Multi-turn Wason-style test: hidden Boolean rule over three numbers, up to 30 test triples, then a guess. Best model solved 14 of 50 rules (28%).
numbers: Accuracy out of 50: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 14, o1-mini 13, o1-preview 12, chatgpt-4o-latest 11, Mistral Large 2 11, GPT-4o 9, Llama 3.1 405B 8, Gemma 2 9B 0.
limits: N=50 rules, one run per model; rules are Python lambdas. The paper's own text says 28%; a later paper quotes 26%.
agent_relevance: Shows how weak model hypothesis testing is; narrowing the hypothesis space by tests is the bottleneck.

source: Banatt, Cheng, Vaidyanath, Hwu (2024) WILT: A Multi-Turn, Memorization-Robust Inductive Logic Benchmark for LLMs
finding: Test proposing and rule deduction are separate skills. o1-mini given the tests proposed by chatgpt-4o-latest guessed 19 of 50 rules, more than any model alone. Sonnet degraded most when its reasoning for each test was stripped.
numbers: o1-mini with GPT-4o-latest tests: 19/50 vs 13/50 alone.
limits: Small-scale cross-model design.
agent_relevance: Splitting 'who proposes the discriminating test' from 'who draws the conclusion' can beat one model doing both; fits S7 where code runs the tests.

source: McCune (2003) Mace4 Reference Manual and Guide (ANL/MCS-TM-264)
finding: Mace4 searches for finite models of first-order formulas: for a domain size n it builds all ground instances and runs a special decision procedure with the least-number heuristic. It is meant to run beside a prover: prover looks for a proof, Mace4 for a countermodel.
numbers: Default domain size 2; iterates upward with iterate_up_to. Example: finds a small non-commutative group from axioms plus 'A*B != B*A'.
quote: a useful complement to first-order theorem provers
limits: Only finite models. First-order satisfiability is not even semidecidable, so no model up to size n is not a proof. Best on equational problems.
agent_relevance: Pattern for S7: search small structures where claim A holds and B fails; failure up to a stated bound is weak evidence only.

source: McCune (2003) Mace4 Reference Manual and Guide (ANL/MCS-TM-264)
finding: Mace4 replaced the earlier SAT-translation (Mace2), which blew up for clauses with many variables or nested terms. For a fixed finite domain, existence of a model is decidable. Builds on FALCON and SEM.
numbers: Domain elements are named 0..n-1.
limits: Design note, no benchmark numbers given in this manual.
agent_relevance: Bounded search is cheap and exact at each size; state the size bound as a budget.

source: Blanchette (2024) Picking Nits: A User's Guide to Nitpick for Isabelle/HOL
finding: Nitpick is a counterexample generator for Isabelle/HOL built on the Kodkod relational model finder. You type 'nitpick' after a putative theorem. For infinite types it can give only 'potentially spurious' counterexamples, and it warns when the conjecture is outside its supported fragment.
numbers: Enumerates cardinalities 1 to 10 for nat by default ('Trying 10 scopes'). Manual: if no genuine counterexample at card nat = k, very unlikely for smaller domains.
quote: Nitpick found a potentially spurious counterexample
limits: Spurious results arise when partial functions appear at the bound (example with + on {0}). Quickcheck can loop and Refute run out of resources on inductive predicates; Nitpick handles least fixed points with its own encoding.
agent_relevance: Label results as genuine, potentially spurious, or none found within scope; never treat none-found as proof.

source: Blanchette and Nipkow (2010) Nitpick: A counterexample generator for higher-order logic based on a relational model finder (ITP 2010)
finding: Founding Nitpick paper. Not opened this session (PDF mirrors returned 404 and web search quota was exhausted); known only through the user guide above.
limits: Not read; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Open before relying on its benchmark comparisons with Refute and Quickcheck.

source: Wagner (2021) Constructions in combinatorics via neural networks
finding: Deep cross-entropy reinforcement learning with no prior knowledge produces explicit counterexamples to several open graph-theory conjectures. The score measures how far a candidate beats the conjectured bound; a positive score means refuted.
numbers: Refuted a question of Brualdi and Cao on permanents of pattern-avoiding matrices and several eigenvalue conjectures (including Aouchiche-Hansen, and Collins's peak-location conjecture in a strong sense).
quote: we did not succeed in refuting any of the most famous conjectures
limits: Author states none of the most famous conjectures was refuted. Works only when a counterexample is a finite object with a computable score.
agent_relevance: Cast a claim as a score that a counterexample would push past zero, then search; needs a checkable score.

source: Charton, Ellenberg, Wagner, Williamson (2024) PatternBoost: Constructions in Mathematics with a Little Help from AI
finding: Alternates local search with a transformer trained on the best finds, and samples from it to seed the next round. It built a counterexample to a 30-year-old conjecture (Graham) on edge-deleted hypercubes.
numbers: d=6: spanning diameter-6 subgraph with 81 edges against the conjectured minimum 82 (2^6 + C(6,3) - 2). For d=5 the conjectured construction looked optimal. No-isosceles grid n=64: 110 points, versus 96 from the best LLM program-search model in Ellenberg et al.
quote: construction of a counterexample to a conjecture that had remained open for 30 years
limits: Strong on problems with cheap scoring and local search; performance varies by problem.
agent_relevance: A learned proposer plus an exact checker: the generator may be noisy, the verifier is not.

source: Ellenberg, Fraser-Taliente, Harvey, Srivastava, Sutherland (2025) Generative Modeling for Mathematical Discovery
finding: Open-source FunSearch-style implementation (LLM writes a priority program, code scores it) on cap sets, narrow admissible tuples and no-isosceles sets. FunSearch originally found a cap set of size 512 in 8 dimensions.
numbers: No-isosceles n=64: best LLM set 96 points vs 110 from PatternBoost.
limits: Authors warn later models may have the record-breaking program in training data.
agent_relevance: LLM-in-the-loop search with an exact evaluator works for constructions but can trail a specialised learned search.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale (AlphaEvolve)
finding: AlphaEvolve (LLM-guided evolutionary code search) was run on 67 problems. On several conjectures it was told to find a counterexample by optimising a score that is negative unless the conjecture breaks. It found none.
numbers: 67 problems. No counterexample for a strengthening of Sendov's conjecture, Duchi's conjecture, a power-of-2 cycle conjecture on graphs up to 40 vertices, or 4-equidistant polygon vertices (reached 3).
limits: The authors do not treat failure as evidence the conjecture holds.
agent_relevance: Report negatives as 'none found within budget X', never as support.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale (AlphaEvolve)
finding: The search repeatedly exploited the checker: loopholes and artifacts when a global constraint was approximated by a discrete check. Score functions were rebuilt to block degenerate cheats.
numbers: Authors describe a 'cheating phenomenon' with leaky verifiers and irregular functions; polygon score normalised by squared minimum side length to stop points collapsing.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: A discriminating test needs an exact verifier; a leaky one turns search into reward hacking (G10).

source: Prasad, Stengel-Eskin, Chen, Khan, Bansal (2025) Learning to Generate Unit Tests for Automated Debugging (UTGen, COLM 2025)
finding: Two goals compete: a test input that breaks the wrong code, and a correct prediction of its expected output without the gold solution. Prompting for failing tests raises attack rate but lowers output accuracy, so the joint score barely moves. UTGen trained on both beats baselines by 7.59%.
numbers: Qwen2.5 7B: prompting for failing tests +13.53 attack rate, -16.47 output accuracy; joint 13.53 vs 14.71. UTGen with UTDebug lifts Qwen2.5 32B pass@1 by over 3.17% (HumanEvalFix) and 12.35% (MBPP+Fix hard); GPT-4o debugging +13.8% with UTGen feedback.
limits: Predicted outputs are noisy, so UTDebug checks edits against several tests and backtracks to avoid fitting a wrong test.
agent_relevance: Without a reference the model's claimed right answer on the discriminating input can be wrong. At S7 choose inputs where candidates differ and settle the answer by running, not by the model's say-so.

source: Prasad, Stengel-Eskin, Chen, Khan, Bansal (2025) Learning to Generate Unit Tests for Automated Debugging (UTGen, COLM 2025)
finding: Generated tests also work as a selector: best-of-10 code selection with UTGen tests beat a trained reward model.
numbers: Beats an 8B reward model by 4.43% on HumanEval+ (Qwen2.5 7B, best-of-10); random tests 3.73% worse, prompted tests 1.83% worse (Llama3 8B).
limits: Code domain only.
agent_relevance: Tests chosen to discriminate beat random tests for selection.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at locating the first mistake in a chain-of-thought trace, yet fix it well when told where it is. Fault location is the hard step; per-step prompting finds mistakes better on wrong traces but flags errors on correct ones.
numbers: Tasks: word sorting, tracking shuffled objects, logical deduction, multistep arithmetic, Dyck languages; 300 traces each, 85% with wrong final answer. Mistake-finding accuracy varies widely by prompting method: e.g. GPT-3.5-Turbo trace-level 3.76 to 10.34 on some tasks vs step-level 35 to 79.
limits: Exact per-cell mapping unverified because the table text is garbled; read as a range only.
agent_relevance: Locate the failure by code (run and diff), then ask for the fix, as in S5.

source: McAleese et al. (2024) LLM Critics Help Catch LLM Bugs (CriticGPT)
finding: RLHF-trained critic LLMs write bug reports on model-written code. Critiques were preferred to human critiques in 63% of cases on naturally occurring bugs. Critics also hallucinate bugs; human-plus-critic teams hallucinate less.
numbers: 63% preferred over human critiques; model critics catch more bugs than paid contractors; found hundreds of errors in data rated flawless; preferred over ChatGPT critiques more than 80% of the time on tampered bugs.
limits: Hallucinated 'nitpick' bugs are a stated cost.
agent_relevance: A critic with no execution tends to invent flaws; ground the S7 challenge in a run so false counterexamples are rejected.
